opus-5.5.text:
I think the right way to think about it is that AI should sit on top of the existing control stack, not replace it. Industrial facilities already have decades of investment in control systems — PLCs, SCADA, building management systems — and those systems are really good at what they were designed to do, which is executing deterministic logic reliably and safely, keeping a valve at a setpoint, tripping a breaker when something goes out of bounds. What they're not good at is optimization across a really complex, nonlinear, constantly changing system. That's where AI comes in.

So the architecture we've found works is a supervisory layer. The AI looks at the whole system, thousands of sensors and how they interact, and figures out what the optimal setpoints should be at any given moment. Then it passes those recommendations down to the existing control system, which actually executes them. The underlying controls stay in charge of the fast, safety-critical loops, and the AI is essentially acting like a very experienced operator who never gets tired and can hold the whole plant in their head at once.

That separation matters a lot for trust and safety. You keep the existing safety interlocks and hard constraints in place, so even if the AI makes a bad recommendation, the system won't do anything dangerous. You layer on additional verification as well, checking every action against operating limits and the plant's own engineering constraints before anything gets sent. And operators always keep the ability to take back control instantly.

It's also why we usually start in an advisory mode, where the AI makes recommendations and humans decide whether to act on them, and only move toward closed-loop autonomous control once the operators have seen it perform and built confidence in it. In heavy industry you can't just ask people to rip out what works and trust a black box. You have to meet them where they are, integrate with what they already have, and earn the right to more autonomy over time.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a supervisory AI layer that sends setpoint recommendations to existing control systems, which execute them.

r002.rationale: The response describes existing controls as deterministic and reliable, but does not say their behavior stays fixed unless their programmed logic is updated.

r003.rationale: The response says existing controls handle deterministic and safety-critical tasks, but does not argue that hardcoded rules and heuristics suffice for most granular control tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I spent years at DeepMind working on data center cooling and then co-founded Phaidra specifically around this question. And my honest view is that AI should not replace the existing control stack. It should sit on top of it.

If you look at any industrial facility — a data center, a pharma plant, a district energy system — there's already a control system in place. You've got PLCs, you've got a building management system, you've got SCADA, and underneath all of that are decades of hard-won safety interlocks and operating constraints. That stuff works. It's deterministic, it's auditable, and the people who run these plants trust it. You don't rip that out.

What that existing layer is bad at is optimization. A PID loop is great at holding a setpoint. It is terrible at deciding what the setpoint should be when you have hundreds of interacting variables, weather changing, load changing, equipment aging, electricity prices moving. Humans end up doing that part, and they do it with rules of thumb that were written down years ago. That's where the AI belongs — as a supervisory layer that's recommending or writing setpoints, while the low-level controllers and the safety systems still do exactly what they've always done.

The second thing I'd say is that trust has to be earned incrementally. When we first did this at Google, the AI wasn't driving anything. It was making recommendations, and operators would look at them and decide whether to act. Only after months of that, when people could see it was consistently right, did we move to closed loop — and even then with hard constraints that the AI could never violate, and a human who could hit the button and fall back to the old control at any time. I think that pattern is the right one everywhere. Start in advisory mode, keep the guardrails outside the model, and let the operators stay in control of how much autonomy they hand over.

And the last piece is that the operators themselves have to be part of it. These are people who know their plant better than any model does. If you show up and say "the AI knows best," you lose them, and frankly you deserve to. If you show up and say "this is a tool that's going to take the tedious part of your job and let you focus on the hard stuff," that lands very differently. The best deployments I've seen are the ones where the operators end up being the biggest advocates.

r001.rationale: The response says AI belongs in a supervisory layer that recommends or writes setpoints, while existing low-level controllers execute them.

r002.rationale: It mentions longstanding safety interlocks and rules of thumb, but does not state that hardcoded behavior stays fixed unless its programmed logic is updated.

r003.rationale: It says the existing control layer works and describes PID loops as useful for holding setpoints, but does not claim hardcoded rules are sufficient for most granular control tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think AI should fit into those systems as another layer of intelligence. Industrial control systems have a lot of engineering built into them, and you want to preserve that. The existing controls handle fast responses and safety interlocks, while AI can look across the system and help determine better operating set points.

Take a cooling system: you might have pumps, fans, and chillers that all interact. Optimizing each piece individually doesn’t necessarily give you the most efficient system overall. AI can help coordinate them, subject to the constraints that operators and engineers establish.

The key is to introduce it gradually. Start with recommendations, let operators understand and validate the behavior, and move toward automation as you build confidence. And if the AI is unavailable or encounters something it can’t handle, the existing control system should continue operating safely.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that hardcoded control behavior remains fixed unless its programmed logic is updated.

r003.rationale: It says existing controls handle fast responses and safety interlocks, but does not argue that hardcoded rules and heuristics suffice for most granular control tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI should fit into those systems as another layer of control. You’ve already got equipment controllers, safety interlocks, and operators who understand the plant. The goal is to give them a system that can look across all that equipment and figure out how to operate it more efficiently, while respecting the constraints they’ve established.

You can start by having the AI make recommendations, so operators can see what it would do and build confidence in it. Then, as you validate its performance, you can give it more authority within a clearly defined operating envelope. And if it encounters a situation it can’t handle, the existing controls should be able to take over. That makes adoption much more practical: you’re improving the system people already trust.
